usage: to be the same as N
하고 = casual 'with/as'; 와/과 is the written equivalent
to seem like N / to be like N
no 하고 here — this means 'resembles', a different sense
examples: 우리 가방이 같아요.
Our bags are the same.
subject takes 이/가; the two items being equated
저하고 나이가 같아요.
We're the same age.
the compared-to person takes 하고, the matching trait takes 가
생각이 저랑 똑같아서 깜짝 놀랐어요.
Your thinking is exactly like mine, so I was startled.
real reaction; 랑 = casual 하고, 똑같다 raises the emphasis
nuance: 같다 says two or more things match or are identical — 'A and B are the same'. To compare, the yardstick noun takes 하고/와·과 and the matching trait takes 이/가: 저하고 키가 같아요 ('our height is the same as mine'). Watch the sharp split from 비슷하다 ('similar'): 같다 means literally no difference, while 비슷하다 allows a gap — friends who 'look alike but aren't twins' are 비슷하다, not 같다. A second trap is the homophone-feeling N 같다 ('seems like N', as in 학생 같아요 'seems to be a student'), which drops 하고 and shifts meaning entirely; 같이 (together / -like) shares the root but is an adverb. English speakers also over-apply 'the same as' with 처럼 — but 처럼 means 'like/as', not 'identical', so keep 같다 for true equality.

Dropping the particle: native Korean is 'A하고 B가 같아요', not 'A B 같아요'. The yardstick needs 하고/와, the trait needs 이/가.

usage: 하고 marks what it differs from; 와/과 in writing
it differs from person to person
examples: 맛이 좀 달라요.
The taste is a bit different.
좀 softens it; note 르-irregular 달라요, not 다라요
저는 생각이 달라요.
I think differently.
lit. 'my thought is different' — Korean states the trait, not the person, as subject
사이즈가 사람마다 달라서 입어 보고 사세요.
Sizes differ per person, so try it on before buying.
real shopping advice; 마다 + 다르다 is idiomatic
nuance: 다르다 is the antonym of 같다 and conjugates as a 르-irregular: the stem 다르 + 아요 doubles the ㄹ and drops 으 to give 달라요 (never 다라요); past is 달랐어요. The pre-noun form 다른 is one of the most-used words in Korean and covers both 'different' and 'another' (다른 색 = 'a different/another colour'). The dangerous trap for English speakers is 틀리다, which means 'to be wrong / incorrect' — even native speakers loosely say 틀리다 for 'different' in speech, but in correct Korean 답이 틀리다 = 'the answer is wrong' while 답이 다르다 = 'the answer is different'. Mixing them can imply someone is mistaken when you only meant they differ, which can sound rude. Pair 다르다 with 하고/와 for the thing compared: 작년하고 달라요 ('it's different from last year').

Conjugating it as 다라요 — it's a 르-irregular, so the correct present form is 달라요 (and past 달랐어요).
Forgetting the comparison particle: say '이거하고 달라요', not '이거 달라요'.

english: to be exactly the same / identical
usage: pre-noun form, e.g. 똑같은 옷 'identical clothes'
adverb — handy for ordering or copying
맨날 'every day' adds a fed-up nuance
examples: 이거하고 똑같아요.
It's exactly the same as this one.
pointing while comparing; 하고 on the reference item
둘이 얼굴이 똑같아요.
The two have identical faces.
둘이 = 'the two of them'; said of twins/look-alikes
앞 사람하고 똑같이 주세요.
Give me exactly the same as the person ahead of me.
real café line; adverb 똑같이 directs the action
nuance: 똑같다 is the emphatic cousin of 같다: the prefix-like 똑 (a mimetic 'precisely / spot-on') pushes 'the same' all the way to 'identical, no difference whatsoever'. Where 같다 can be a calm statement of equality, 똑같다 adds feeling — surprise at a resemblance, or, with words like 맨날 ('every day'), boredom that nothing changes. It dominates everyday speech far more than its formal feel suggests. The adverb 똑같이 ('identically / the same way') is genuinely useful for service situations ('make mine 똑같이'). Beware the same particle trap as 같다: the reference noun needs 하고/와, so 저거하고 똑같아요, not 저거 똑같아요. And don't reach for 똑같다 when things are only roughly alike — that gap is 비슷하다 territory; 똑같다 insists they are indistinguishable.

usage: ㅂ-irregular pre-noun form, e.g. 아름다운 풍경
adverb form, e.g. 아름답게 꾸미다 'decorate beautifully'
참 'truly' gives a soft, admiring tone
examples: 바다가 아름다워요.
The sea is beautiful.
scenery is the prototypical subject; note ㅂ-irregular 아름다워요
아름다운 노래예요.
It's a beautiful song.
pre-noun 아름다운 before the noun
노을이 너무 아름다워서 한참 서 있었어요.
The sunset was so beautiful I stood there a long while.
real moment; 아서 links beauty to the resulting action
nuance: 아름답다 is the 'proper', somewhat literary word for beautiful, reserved most often for scenery, nature, music, art, a person's heart, or a moving moment rather than everyday cuteness. It is a ㅂ-irregular adjective: the final ㅂ turns to 우 before a vowel, giving 아름다워요 / 아름다운 / 아름다워서 (never 아름답어요). The key boundary for learners is 예쁘다: in casual speech, a pretty face, a cute café, or a nice dress is 예쁘다, while 아름답다 sounds more elevated and emotional — calling a snack 아름답다 sounds odd, but a mountain view is 아름답다. 예쁘다 leans 'pretty/cute', 아름답다 leans 'beautiful/sublime'. Note also 곱다 (refined, graceful beauty, often of older speech), which is gentler and more old-fashioned. Use 아름답다 to admire the grand or heartfelt, and don't force it onto small, cute, or tasty things.

usage: pre-noun form, e.g. 훌륭한 작품 'an excellent work'
adverb, e.g. 훌륭하게 해내다 'pull it off splendidly'
common praise of a person's integrity
examples: 음식이 정말 훌륭해요.
The food is truly excellent.
praising a meal a notch above 맛있어요
훌륭한 선생님이에요.
She's an excellent teacher.
pre-noun form praising ability and character
어린 나이에 정말 훌륭하게 컸네요.
You've grown up so admirably for your age.
real compliment to a young person; adverb 훌륭하게
nuance: 훌륭하다 is high, somewhat formal praise for quality, ability, or moral character — 'excellent, admirable, fine, splendid'. It sits clearly above 좋다 ('good'): 좋다 is everyday and broad, while 훌륭하다 implies something genuinely impressive and worthy of respect, so it shines in reviews, classrooms, and sincere compliments about work, skill, or a person's integrity (인격이 훌륭하다). Compare it with 대단하다: 대단하다 is a hot, spoken 'wow, impressive!' reaction to an achievement, whereas 훌륭하다 is a calmer, more considered verdict on worth — a child's drawing earns 대단하다 in the moment but a master's life work earns 훌륭하다. As a 하다-adjective it conjugates regularly (훌륭해요 / 훌륭했어요) and, being descriptive, takes the pre-noun -ㄴ: 훌륭한 사람, never 훌륭하는 사람. Don't sprinkle it on trivial 'nice' situations, where it can sound grandiose.

Forming the pre-noun as 훌륭하는 N — adjectives use -ㄴ/은, so it's 훌륭한 N (the -는 form is for verbs).
Treating 훌륭하다 and 대단하다 as interchangeable; 훌륭하다 is a measured judgement of worth, while 대단하다 is a spontaneous 'wow' reaction.

usage: pre-noun form, e.g. 대단한 실력 'amazing skill'
a big deal / a serious matter
진짜 = casual 'really', very common in reactions
it's not that big a deal
examples: 와, 정말 대단해요!
Wow, that's really amazing!
spontaneous admiration; 와 sets the reaction tone
대단한 실력이에요.
That's an amazing skill.
실력 = skill/ability, a classic partner noun
혼자 그걸 다 했다고요? 진짜 대단해요!
You did all that by yourself? You're really amazing!
real praise of effort; 다고요 shows surprised confirmation
nuance: 대단하다 is the everyday go-to compliment — 'impressive, amazing, remarkable' — usually aimed at a person's achievement, effort, or ability, and it carries warm, spoken energy (often opened with 와 or 진짜). Set against 훌륭하다, 대단하다 is the hotter, more emotional in-the-moment reaction ('wow, you're amazing!'), while 훌륭하다 is a cooler verdict on worth; you'd gush 대단하다 at someone who just aced a race, but reserve 훌륭하다 for praising their character or a polished body of work. A second sense surfaces with a flat tone: 대단한 일 = 'a big/serious matter', and the modest deflection 별로 대단한 일 아니에요 means 'it's no big deal'. Watch the adverb 대단히 ('very, greatly', as in 대단히 감사합니다) — it modifies other words and is not the same as the adjective. Also, aim 대단하다 at others; using it on your own success sounds boastful.

usage: pre-noun form, e.g. 평범한 회사원 'an ordinary office worker'
지극히 'extremely' is the idiomatic intensifier here
adverb 평범하게 + 살다, a common life-goal phrase
일상 'daily life' is a frequent partner noun
examples: 저는 평범한 학생이에요.
I'm an ordinary student.
modest self-description, a very natural use
맛은 좀 평범해요.
The taste is kind of ordinary.
honest, mild review; 좀 softens it
남들처럼 평범하게 살고 싶어요.
I just want to live an ordinary life like everyone else.
heartfelt wish; adverb 평범하게 + 처럼 'like'
nuance: 평범하다 (平凡, 平 'flat/level' + 凡 'ordinary') means 'ordinary, average, nothing special', and it is essentially neutral, not an insult — Koreans use it modestly about themselves or their routines, and 'I want a 평범한 life' is a sincere, even wistful wish. Its sharp antonym is 특별하다 ('special'), and it overlaps with 흔하다 ('common') but from a different angle: 평범하다 judges character/quality ('unremarkable, run-of-the-mill'), while 흔하다 judges frequency ('found everywhere'). So a name can be 흔하다 (lots of people have it) and a person 평범하다 (an average sort) — they aren't swappable. Tone decides the colour: said warmly it's humble; said with a sigh it edges toward 'mediocre/disappointing'. As a 하다-adjective it takes the pre-noun -ㄴ (평범한 사람, not 평범하는 사람) and the adverb 평범하게.

usage: pre-noun form, e.g. 흔한 이름 'a common name'
negated, a frequent way to say 'rare'
adverb, e.g. 흔히 쓰는 말 'a commonly used phrase'
to be dirt-common / a dime a dozen
흔해 빠지다 adds a dismissive nuance
examples: 그 이름은 아주 흔해요.
That name is very common.
talking about frequency of a name
여기서는 흔한 일이에요.
It's a common thing around here.
일 = thing/occurrence; 여기서는 'around here'
이런 디자인은 흔해서 별로 안 끌려요.
This kind of design is so common it doesn't appeal to me.
real opinion; here 흔하다 carries the 'unoriginal' shade
nuance: 흔하다 means something is common, plentiful, easily found, or seen everywhere — its core is frequency/availability. Its direct antonym is 드물다 ('rare, scarce'), and the negated 흔하지 않다 is a natural way to say 'uncommon'. The line to draw is against 평범하다: 흔하다 = 'occurs a lot / is everywhere' (a 흔한 성씨, a common surname), whereas 평범하다 = 'is unremarkable in quality' (a 평범한 영화, an average movie); a thing can be one without the other. Tone gives 흔하다 two flavours: neutrally it just means 'widely available' (마트에서 흔하게 팔아요), but about taste or style it can turn faintly negative — 'too common, unoriginal', as in 흔한 디자인. The adverb is 흔히 ('commonly, often'), as in 흔히 볼 수 있어요. English speakers sometimes reach for 흔하다 to describe a plain personality — but a person's ordinariness is 평범하다, not 흔하다.

usage: pre-noun form, e.g. 소중한 추억 'a precious memory'
여기다 'to consider' is a natural partner
to be precious above all else
examples: 가족이 제일 소중해요.
Family is the most precious.
제일 = most; emotional value, not price
소중한 친구예요.
She's a precious friend.
pre-noun form on a relationship
네가 준 편지, 아직도 소중하게 간직하고 있어.
I still treasure the letter you gave me.
real heartfelt line; 소중하게 + 간직하다 'keep dear'
nuance: 소중하다 (所重, 'that which is weighty/important') describes something dear and treasured — people, time, memories, relationships, a meaningful gift — measuring worth to the heart, not price in money. Keep it apart from two neighbours: 비싸다 is about cost ('expensive'), and 귀하다 is closer but leans 'rare/precious because scarce or noble' (귀한 손님 'an honoured guest'), while 소중하다 is the emotional 'dear to me'. So a cheap toy from a late grandparent is 소중하다 even though it's not 비싸다. It carries warm, sincere feeling, which makes it a lovely word for cards, letters, and heartfelt moments (시간이 소중하다 'time is precious'; 너는 나에게 소중한 사람이야 'you're precious to me'). The adverb 소중히/소중하게 pairs with verbs like 간직하다 ('keep dear') and 여기다 ('regard'). As a 하다-adjective the pre-noun is 소중한, never 소중하는.

Forming the pre-noun as 소중하는 N — adjectives take -ㄴ, so it's 소중한 N (소중한 사람).

usage: the thing you're accustomed to takes 에, not 을/를
to get the hang of (by hand)
related idiom from the 익- root, for skills
pre-noun form, e.g. 익숙한 얼굴 'a familiar face'
examples: 이제 일에 익숙해요.
I'm used to the work now.
이제 = now; 일 takes 에
익숙한 길이에요.
It's a familiar road.
pre-noun form describing a known route
한국 생활에 익숙해지는 데 1년쯤 걸렸어요.
It took about a year to get used to life in Korea.
real settling-in line; 익숙해지다 + 데 'the process of'
nuance: 익숙하다 means 'familiar / accustomed to' — something you've done or seen enough that it now feels easy and natural. The crucial grammar point is the particle: the thing you're used to is marked with 에 (not 을/를), so 운전에 익숙해요 ('I'm used to driving'), 분위기에 익숙해요 ('used to the atmosphere'). Its antonym is 낯설다 ('unfamiliar, strange'), and to say you gradually get accustomed you switch to the 'becoming' verb 익숙해지다. Distinguish it from 친숙하다, which adds an affectionate 'close/cosy' warmth (a 친숙한 멜로디 feels endearing), whereas 익숙하다 is the neutral 'this is routine for me'. The 익- root also gives 익다 ('to ripen / be cooked', as in 고기가 익다), so don't let the shared syllable confuse the meanings. 익숙하다 is invaluable for talking about settling into a new job, city, or life.

usage: pre-noun form, e.g. 분명한 이유 'a clear reason'
adverb — even more common than the adjective in speech
expresses the speaker's certainty about a past act
examples: 이유가 분명해요.
The reason is clear.
이유 = reason; the matter is unambiguous
분명한 대답을 주세요.
Please give me a clear answer.
pre-noun form requesting a definite reply
분명히 여기에 뒀는데 왜 없지?
I definitely put it right here, so why is it gone?
real puzzled moment; 분명히 voices the speaker's certainty
nuance: 분명하다 (分明, 分 'divide' + 明 'bright/clear') means something is clear, definite, and unambiguous — used for reasons, answers, facts, intentions, and stances (입장이 분명하다 'one's position is clear'). In everyday speech the adverb 분명히 ('clearly / surely / definitely') is even more frequent, often broadcasting the speaker's own certainty: 분명히 잠갔어요 ('I definitely locked it'). The fine line is against 확실하다: 분명하다 stresses that something is objectively obvious/unmistakable, while 확실하다 stresses the speaker's subjective confidence that it's true — '증거가 분명하다' (the evidence is clear-cut) vs '나는 확실해' (I'm sure). A second, separate word is 선명하다, which is visual sharpness — a 선명한 사진 ('a vivid, crisp photo') or clear sound; you can't use 분명하다 for image clarity. Note also that the natural adverb is 분명히, not 분명하게, in most speech.

usage: pre-noun form, e.g. 확실한 증거 'solid evidence'
negated form, a soft way to express doubt
to make sure / nail it down
examples: 그건 확실해요.
That's certain.
그건 = 'as for that'; speaker is sure
확실한 약속이에요?
Is it a firm promise?
pre-noun form checking reliability
내일 오는 거 확실해요? 일정 바꿔도 돼요?
Are you sure you're coming tomorrow? Can I change my schedule?
real confirmation; 확실해요? checks the other person's certainty
nuance: 확실하다 (確實, 確 'firm/sure' + 實 'real/true') expresses certainty and confidence — you're sure something is true, settled, or reliable. The adverb 확실히 ('certainly, definitely, for sure') is very common when answering or confirming (확실히 그래요 'that's definitely so'). The sharp contrast is with 분명하다: 확실하다 centres on the speaker's subjective confidence ('I'm sure of it'), while 분명하다 centres on a thing being objectively obvious/unambiguous — so 나는 확실해 ('I'm certain') but 증거가 분명해 ('the evidence is clear-cut'). It also brushes against 틀림없다 ('there's no mistake / definitely'), which is even more emphatic. Crucially, 확실하다 is for certainty, not possibility: to say 'maybe' you need 아마 ('probably') or '-ㄹ지도 몰라요' ('might'), not 확실하다. The natural adverb is 확실히 in everyday speech (확실하게 is a touch stiffer).

usage: drops 이/가 in shop talk, e.g. 예약 가능해요?
set frame, e.g. 가능한 한 빨리 'as soon as possible'
the noun derived from the same 가능 root
examples: 오늘 배달 가능해요?
Is delivery possible today?
asking at a shop; 배달 가능해요? is a fixed service phrase
환불 가능해요.
A refund is possible.
환불 = refund; the noun stands directly before 가능하다
가능하면 회의를 오전으로 옮길 수 있을까요?
If possible, could we move the meeting to the morning?
real polite request; 가능하면 cushions the ask
nuance: 가능하다 (可能, 可 'can/permissible' + 能 'ability') means 'possible / doable / available', and it is wonderfully practical for daily service questions — 예약 가능해요? ('Is a reservation possible?'), 카드 가능해요? ('Can I pay by card?'). In these, a noun sits directly before it and it neatly replaces a longer '-ㄹ 수 있다' clause, sounding crisp and businesslike. The softener 가능하면 ('if possible') makes requests polite, and the fixed frame 가능한 한 + adjective/adverb means 'as ~ as possible' (가능한 한 빨리 'as soon as possible') — note this is different from 가능한 N ('a possible N'). Its antonym is 불가능하다. One pitfall: while 가능하다 and '-ㄹ 수 있다' both render English 'can', '-ㄹ 수 있다' attaches to a verb stem describing an action you're able to do (갈 수 있어요 'I can go'), whereas 가능하다 attaches to a noun or stands alone judging feasibility — don't merge them into 갈 가능해요.

usage: 사실상 'in effect' adds a formal nuance
pre-noun form, e.g. 불가능한 일 'an impossible task'
examples: 오늘은 예약이 불가능해요.
A reservation isn't possible today.
polite refusal; the matter takes 이/가 here
그건 좀 불가능해요.
That's a bit impossible.
좀 softens the 'no' — a very Korean cushioning
환불은 불가능하지만 교환은 가능해요.
A refund isn't possible, but an exchange is.
real shop reply; 은/는 contrasts refund vs exchange
nuance: 불가능하다 (不可能, the prefix 不 'not/un-' on 가능 'possible') is the direct antonym of 가능하다: 불 flips it to 'cannot be done, impossible'. For an everyday personal 'I can't', the '-ㄹ 수 없다' pattern (갈 수 없어요 'I can't go') is more natural than forcing 불가능하다, which leans toward declaring something infeasible in principle. As a 하다-adjective the pre-noun is 불가능한, never 불가능하는.
